questions.prompt:

Jack's new job requires heavy lift. He will have to take care of his back.

questions.passage: Bushfires are a cause of major concern during the summer months in Australia. It is not uncommon for total fire bans to be announced to aid the prevention of many spot fires, for many fires are started by people being careless when the weather is hot. Although it is the firefighters who ultimately put out the fires, everyone has a responsibility to make sure they are doing everything they can to help prevent fires which can damage property and acres of land.
questions.prompt: What can you infer from this paragraph?

options.label: A
options.text: People living in the city are not affected by bushfires.

options.label: B
options.text: All bushfires are started by people.

options.label: C
options.text: It is everybody's responsibility to help prevent bushfires.

options.label: D
options.text: Bushfires are the sole responsibility of firefighters.

questions.explanation: The passage says "everyone has a responsibility to make sure they are doing everything they can to help prevent fires". It does not say who is affected (A), only that "many" fires — not all — are started by people (B), and it says firefighters are not solely responsible (D).

questions.passage: With the ferocity of a lion, yet the size of a wombat, the Honey Badger is one of the toughest mammals in Africa and Western Asia. Honey badgers stand less than one foot high and are less than a metre long and they weigh around ten kilos. Despite this they have a reputation for toughness that is far greater than their size. They also have an exceptionally thick, loose skin, which makes them difficult to grip on to, and which is almost impenetrable to bites, arrows and spears. Some Honey Badgers have been known to chase away lions and take their kill. I guess size isn't everything when it comes to a fight.

options.text: What makes Honey Badgers so tough is their speed and strength.

options.label: B
options.text: Honey Badgers are large and tireless in fighting.

options.label: C
options.text: Honey Badgers get their name from their love of honey.

options.label: D
options.text: Their thick, loose skin is what makes Honey Badgers so tough.

options.label: E
options.text: Honey Badgers have sweet tasting meat, hence the name.

questions.explanation: The passage attributes their toughness and their protection against bites, arrows and spears to their thick, loose skin.

questions.passage: His bedroom was strewn with dirty clothing, half-drunk cups of tea and piles of books. questions.passage:
Seals are warm blooded, hairy mammals perfectly evolved for life in the sea. Water takes more heat from a body than air does, so seals have developed a layer of tough, spongy tissue filled with oily fat just beneath their skin. This tissue, called blubber, keeps in body heat and allows them to spend time in icy waters in the Arctic and around the globe. Seals are incredible swimmers, perfectly adapted to catching fish as they swim underwater, holding their breath for up to thirty minutes at a time.

Historically, seals were an important resource for the Inuit people in the Arctic Circle. They were captured for their meat, and for the oil in their blubber, which was used for cooking, lighting and heating. Their skins were made into warm clothing and shelters; and sinews were used for sewing. Seal bones were used to make spears and arrows. Seals are still hunted today, although they are protected in many countries. They are highly intelligent animals who can learn tricks and are often very popular attractions at zoos and wildlife parks.
questions.prompt: Which of these statements follows?

options.label: B
options.text: Without seals the Inuit culture could not have survived.

options.label: C
options.text: Seals are well suited to their environment.

options.label: D
options.text: The bones of seals are the best materials to make spears and arrows with.

options.label: E
options.text: Their ability to perform tricks is why seals are kept in zoos.

questions.explanation: The passage says seals are "perfectly evolved for life in the sea" and "perfectly adapted", which supports that they are well suited to their environment.

questions.passage: At the end of Matthew's street is an old, large house. Many of the children in the street have told Matthew that the house is haunted, and that people who enter the house after sunset never come back out. Although Matthew's dad had told him that there was no such thing as ghosts, he was still convinced that there was something creepy about the house at the end of the street. One afternoon, Matthew and the other children in the street were playing cricket, and Matthew hit the ball so hard it smashed into the front window of the house at the end of the street. The other children were so scared that they all ran home, leaving Matthew out in the street on his own. Matthew knew that the most responsible thing to do was to go to the house and apologise for breaking the window, so he slowly walked up the steps and knocked on the door. To his surprise, a little old lady answered the door and invited him inside. After Matthew apologised for the window and cleaned up the broken glass, the lady thanked him for being honest and offered him a tall glass of milk and some biscuits, before giving him his ball back.
questions.prompt: The main theme of this story is:

options.label: D
options.text: the best way to be responsible is to run away.

questions.explanation: The house that seemed haunted from the rumours turned out to belong to a friendly old lady, showing that appearances and assumptions can be misleading.
